cross_stage_inconsistencies.description: Indonesia sugar mill count — refinement not merged into artifact

Stage 4 refinements file documents the correct figure as 59 active pabrik gula (Kemenperin 2023), with the 69 figure arising from double-counting 11 refining factories that do not use bagasse-fired boilers. The corrected figure with 59 mills shifts the Indonesia sugar contribution from 69×3–5=207–345 boilers to 59×1.3=77 boilers (using Stage 4 refinement's recommended 1.3 boiler/mill multiplier). This materially affects total install-base estimates downstream.

Additionally clarifies that the original 7.4% was incorrectly attributed to 'CIDB' — CIDB is Malaysian, not Indonesian; the Indonesian body is LPJK. cross_stage_inconsistencies.description: PP4.5 (Stage 4) and PP5.3 (Stage 5) cover the same water treatment gap from different vantage points — framing is consistent but cite different cost quantification approaches
cross_stage_inconsistencies.detail: PP4.5 (Stage 4) frames the water treatment gap from the end-user perspective (efficiency loss, fuel overconsumption). PP5.3 (Stage 5) frames it from the service provider perspective (uneconomic minimum viable program cost, transactional vs. managed service). These are complementary and intentionally different. However the cost figures quoted differ slightly: PP4.5 uses aquaphoenix.com (1 mm scale = 10–15% efficiency loss) and beta.co.id (1/8 inch = 20–25%), while PP5.3 uses the same beta.co.id figure plus an additional study (0.3 mm scale = 6.25pp thermal efficiency reduction). The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors (nationalboard.org) independently confirms the 20–25% figure (cited in Stage 5 VC5-act3-1) — this provides genuine cross-validation of the 1/8 inch figure. The framing is consistent and the cost quantification is aligned between stages.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.action_required: No inconsistency. Recommend synthesis document explicitly notes that the National Board citation in Stage 5 independently validates the efficiency loss figure used in Stage 4 PP4.5 — this cross-validation is currently not surfaced in either artifact.

The effect on the $40M–$520M range is proportionally small given the wide uncertainty bands. However the 69 figure is factually wrong in the un-merged artifact.

novel_findings.finding: PP4.5 — Water treatment as systemic efficiency gap in SEA palm oil mill boilers
novel_findings.basis: Three independent primary-academic sources from different Malaysian institutions (UTM Perak 37-mill survey / 1,427 DOSH data points, USM Perak BFW study, AIP Conference Proceedings 2023). Multiple feedwater parameters — pH, hardness, silica, iron — routinely fall outside ASME BPV Section I guidelines across Malaysian palm oil mill population. Scale-induced efficiency losses 10–28% documented. No prior coverage in original pain-point template.
novel_findings.confidence: Medium-High (academic anchor strong; cost quantification via beta.co.id/Lautan Air vendor blog remains the weakest link)

novel_findings.finding: PP5.5 — Malaysia SSI 2025 compliance cliff for small operators
novel_findings.basis: OSH (Plant Requiring Certificate of Fitness) Regulations 2024 / SSI 2025 scheme effective January 21, 2025. Facilities with risk-based internal inspection teams can extend CF from 15 months to up to 60 months. Small operators without such teams are locked into the annual certification cycle, creating a regulatory bifurcation: large operators reduce compliance burden; small operators face proportionally higher fixed compliance costs. Three independent secondary-trade sources (Skrine law firm, Lexology, Advanced HSE Solutions) confirm.
novel_findings.confidence: Medium (three secondary-trade, not yet primary DOSH gazette)

novel_findings.finding: Japan METI FIT discontinuation (≥10 MW large-scale biomass) from FY2026 — demand cliff for Vietnam pellets and Indonesia PKS
novel_findings.basis: METI official English press release 21 March 2025; Argus Media corroboration; METI Santeii Committee working document. New large-scale woody biomass projects (≥10 MW) and all liquid biomass projects will not receive FIT/FIP from FY2026. Existing 20-year legacy contracts continue. Sub-10 MW rate unchanged at ¥24/kWh.
novel_findings.confidence: High (METI primary source + two independent corroborations)

novel_findings.confidence: Medium (Kemenperin primary-ministry + Badan Pangan Nasional + USDA FAS corroboration; boiler multiplier 1.3/mill remains assumed)

top_3_high_confidence_findings.finding: Japan METI has officially discontinued FIT/FIP support for new large-scale (≥10 MW) biomass power projects from FY2026 onward (March 21, 2025 announcement), ending the demand pipeline for imported Vietnam wood pellets and Indonesia/Malaysia PKS in new-build plants. Legacy fleet on 20-year contracts (~2012–2025 vintage) continues to drive existing import demand for the remainder of their contract terms.
top_3_high_confidence_findings.source_quality: High — METI official English press release (primary-ministry), Argus Media corroboration (primary-research-firm), USDA GAIN Japan Biomass 2023
top_3_high_confidence_findings.commercial_implication: Biomass fuel suppliers with contract exposure to Japanese legacy fleet have 5–15 year runway of existing demand. New-build export demand growth is structural zero after FY2026 for large-scale. Domestic SEA co-firing and small-scale (<10 MW) uses are the residual growth market.

top_3_high_confidence_findings.finding: Multiple feedwater parameters (pH, total hardness, silica, iron, phosphate) in Malaysian palm oil mill boilers routinely fall outside ASME BPV Section I guidelines, confirmed across three independent academic studies covering 37 mills and 1,427 DOSH data points. Scale-induced efficiency losses of 10–28% are documented. The water treatment program at most small-to-mid-size operators is managed by generalist boiler operators without specialist water chemistry training.
top_3_high_confidence_findings.source_quality: Medium-High — three independent primary-academic sources: UTM Perak (MJFAS 2022), USM Perak (ESAR 2021), AIP Conference Proceedings 2023
top_3_high_confidence_findings.commercial_implication: Managed water treatment service gap across SEA palm oil and food manufacturing boiler fleet is real, academically confirmed, and not reflected in any market-sizing data reviewed. Entry point for managed water treatment as a service vs. commodity chemical sales.

top_3_high_confidence_findings.finding: Indonesia's ratio of labor inspectors to enterprises is 1:57,000 — approximately 3× below the ILO recommended ratio of 1:20,000 — confirmed by ILO factsheet and Kemnaker OSH Profile 2022. The Kelas I certified boiler operator pool was 4,068 nationally as of 2017 (most recent Kemnaker enumeration available). Against an estimated installed base of ~5,000–8,000 boilers in Indonesia alone requiring certified attendance, the structural shortage of licensed operators is independently confirmed by two primary sources.
top_3_high_confidence_findings.source_quality: High — ILO factsheet (primary-multilateral) + Kemnaker OSH Profile 2022 (primary-ministry); 4,068 operator figure is 2017 data (stale for headcount but structurally corroborated by the inspector ratio)
top_3_high_confidence_findings.commercial_implication: Remote certified operator deployment is the primary recurring revenue model enabler for an aftermarket service entrant in Indonesia. Scarcity is structural, not cyclical.

top_3_questions_for_field_validation.question: What fraction of palm oil mill and small industrial boiler customers in Indonesia and Malaysia have a formal water treatment monitoring program versus reactive treatment or chemical commodity purchases? Have treatment program adherence rates visibly changed during fuel cost pressure periods?
top_3_questions_for_field_validation.why_critical: PP4.5 and PP5.3 rest on the behavioral assumption that small operators manage water treatment poorly. The academic evidence confirms the technical gap (out-of-spec feedwater) but does not directly document operator decision-making or program penetration rates. A single interview with PT Kurita Indonesia or Nalco Water Malaysia commercial team would provide the penetration rate and price-sensitivity data needed to convert PP4.5 from a Medium academic finding to a quantified market opportunity.
top_3_questions_for_field_validation.interview_target: PT Kurita Indonesia sales/commercial director; Nalco Water / Ecolab Malaysia country manager; Lautan Air Indonesia technical director

top_3_questions_for_field_validation.question: What are actual spare parts lead times experienced by maintenance managers in Indonesia and Malaysia for tube bundles, refractory tiles, and grate bars from Chinese and Indian OEM origins — specifically from order placement to parts-on-site?
top_3_questions_for_field_validation.why_critical: PP2.4 and PP5.4 both quantify spare parts lead times using a single vendor blog (coalbiomassboiler.com) that quotes fabrication time only, not customer-experienced total lead time including ocean freight, customs, and inland logistics. Stage 5 DR's correction (10–20 weeks customer-experienced vs. 6–12 weeks fabrication-only) is analytically grounded but not field-validated. The downtime cost argument ($50K–$170K/day) multiplied by a 10–22 week wait is the single largest quantified pain in the corpus — it deserves a primary field source.
top_3_questions_for_field_validation.interview_target: Mechmar Services Malaysia procurement manager; PT Atmindo Indonesia spares team; PTPN or FELDA procurement manager for boiler parts

top_3_questions_for_field_validation.question: How does the Malaysian OSH SSI 2025 scheme (effective January 21, 2025) in practice affect the compliance cost and inspection scheduling for small and mid-size industrial boiler operators — and has the extended 60-month CF pathway been accessed by any palm oil mill or food processing facility?
top_3_questions_for_field_validation.why_critical: PP5.5 identifies the SSI 2025 as a compliance cliff for small operators (who cannot access the extended CF without a risk-based inspection team). The finding is Medium-confidence based on three secondary-trade sources. No primary DOSH gazette has been directly cited, and no operator interview has confirmed actual uptake or access barriers. If the 60-month pathway is practically inaccessible for sub-25 t/h boiler operators, it validates the pain point. If it is accessible with modest investment, the pain point weakens.
top_3_questions_for_field_validation.interview_target: DOSH Malaysia Pressure Vessels and Boilers unit; TÜV Rheinland Malaysia authorized inspection team; Boilermech or ENCO Systems compliance manager dealing with SSI 2025 implementation

gate_reasoning: The full 5-stage corpus — 463 claims across Fuel Suppliers, Boiler OEMs, EPC, Industrial End Users, and Aftermarket — enters final gate scoring at 63.7% Low confidence post-deep-research, placing it firmly within the 30–70% band that triggers ship_with_flag rather than rerun. This is an honest ship_with_flag, not a borderline call. Three factors support shipping: (1) All five stages have completed per-stage validation passes and the 13 DR calls have meaningfully moved anchor claims — Japan METI primary sourcing, EPPO Thailand primary statistics, MPOB oil extraction data, WITS/Comtrade unit values, US DOE lifecycle cost triangulation, EPA equipment cost data, and PUPR construction certification data are all primary-quality additions that were absent in first-pass drafts. (2) The High and Medium confidence claims (36 High, 132 Medium = 36% of corpus) include the structurally critical anchors: regulatory frameworks across three jurisdictions, market-size figures for Malaysia palm oil and Thailand sugar, the Japan FIT discontinuation, ILO inspector-to-enterprise ratio, and the water treatment academic evidence base — these provide a credible factual backbone. (3) Stage 4 is genuinely well-evidenced (57.8% Low post-DR) and Stage 4's PP4.5 water treatment finding is the corpus's most novel and best-sourced insight. Six specific flags must accompany any downstream use. Flag 1: coalbiomassboiler.com is the sole quantitative source for O&M cost percentages (Stages 2, 3) and emissions retrofit costs (Stages 2, 3) that were not displaced by DR — these are explicitly Low-confidence vendor-sourced figures. Flag 2: The Lautan Air / beta.co.id downtime cost figure (RM 228,000–630,000/hr, or ~$50K–$170K/day at 2024 CPO) is the primary severity anchor for 4 pain points across Stages 4 and 5; it has a vendor commercial interest conflict and is unvalidated by any independent source. Flag 3: The Indonesia sugar mill count in stage-4-value-chain.md artifact has not been corrected from 69 to 59 following the DR — this correction must be merged before the artifact is used for market sizing. Flag 4: The Indonesia construction certification rate figure (7.4% in Stage 4) coexists with the corrected Stage 3 figure (4.86%) without cross-reference — synthesis must use the most recent LPJK 2024 data. Flag 5: Approximately 65–75 ASSUMED-N tags across the corpus identify claims with zero source backing; these are particularly concentrated in cost-bottom-up estimates (mobilization costs, re-commissioning costs, agent commission economics) and represent the irreducible research gap that requires operator field interviews. Flag 6: All market sizing claims across all stages are anchored on secondary market research firms (GrandView, TechSci, Inkwood, DataBridge) or APAC-as-proxy figures — no primary government statistics confirm any country-specific boiler market size. The TAM/SAM framing requires a disclosed 'Low confidence' caveat.
